makes.blurb: The best-selling carmaker on Earth. Built its name on durability, then proved it could do excitement too, the 2000GT, the Supra, and a Land Cruiser that outlasts its owners.
makes.knownFor: Reliability, hybrids, the Land Cruiser
makes.name: Toyota
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Johannes Maximilian, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: An engine company that happens to build cars. VTEC, the NSX, and a Civic for every budget and every era of a driver's life.
makes.knownFor: VTEC engines, the NSX, motorcycle-grade engineering
makes.name: Honda
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: Home of Godzilla. The GT-R line spent five decades embarrassing supercars, and the Z car made performance democratic.
makes.knownFor: GT-R, the Z cars, the Skyline lineage
makes.name: Nissan
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: The small company that bet on rotary engines and lightweight roadsters when nobody else would. The MX-5 is the best-selling two-seat sports car in history.
makes.knownFor: MX-5 Miata, rotary engines, driver-first tuning
makes.name: Mazda
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Chris Woodrich, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: All-wheel drive and boxer engines, everywhere, always. Rally stages made the WRX a legend; the Outback made wagons into a lifestyle.
makes.knownFor: Symmetrical AWD, rally heritage, boxer engines
makes.name: Subaru
makes.photoCaption: WRX STI (VA), rally-prepared example in competition livery
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Yu Chu Chin, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: The fastest climb in the industry, from budget punchline in the 1990s to design-led EVs and the N performance division that embarrasses hot hatches twice its price.
makes.knownFor: Ioniq 5, N performance cars, value engineering
makes.name: Hyundai
makes.photoCaption: Ioniq 5, rear 3/4, plugged in at a charger
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Alexander-93, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: Put the world on wheels with the Model T, then gave it the Mustang and the F-Series. The company that beat Ferrari at Le Mans out of spite.
makes.knownFor: Mustang, F-Series trucks, the Model T
makes.name: Ford
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Matti Blume, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: GM's volume brand and America's performance bargain. The Corvette has been the attainable supercar since 1953; the small-block V8 powered everything.
makes.knownFor: Corvette, Camaro, small-block V8
makes.name: Chevrolet
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: Born for war, kept for weekends. The Wrangler is the direct descendant of the Willys MB, and the seven-slot grille is the most copied face in off-roading.
makes.knownFor: Wrangler, trail capability, the original SUV
makes.name: Jeep
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Dinkun Chen, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: Forced the entire industry to go electric. The Model S proved EVs could be the fast option; the Model Y became the best-selling car in the world, of any kind.
makes.knownFor: Electric range and charging network, direct sales
makes.name: Tesla
makes.photoCredit: Photo: AuHaidhausen, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: Started with aircraft engines, defined the sports sedan with the 3 Series, and built the M division into a byword for fast cars that still steer properly.
makes.knownFor: 3 Series, M cars, inline-six engines
makes.name: BMW
makes.photoCaption: BMW M3 (E30) Peter Brock Mobil race car
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Yu Chu Chin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: Benz built the first automobile in 1886 and the company has been previewing the industry's future in the S-Class ever since. The 300SL is the collector benchmark.
makes.knownFor: S-Class, 300SL Gullwing, luxury and safety firsts
makes.name: Mercedes-Benz
makes.photoCaption: 300 SL roadster, hood open, indoor show
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Matti Blume, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: One car, perfected for sixty years: the 911. Around it, Porsche built the most profitable sports-car company in the world without diluting the recipe.
makes.knownFor: 911, motorsport dominance, engineering discipline
makes.name: Porsche
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Matti Blume, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: The people's car, literally. The Beetle is one of the best-selling designs ever; the Golf GTI invented the hot hatch; the Bus became a cultural era on wheels.
makes.knownFor: Beetle, Golf GTI, the Bus
makes.name: Volkswagen
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Greg Gjerdingen, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: Quattro all-wheel drive changed rallying forever in 1980, then changed road cars. Audi sells technology and restraint in equal measure.
makes.knownFor: Quattro AWD, interiors, Le Mans diesel era
makes.name: Audi
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Anna, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: A racing team that sells road cars to fund itself, and has never once pretended otherwise. V12s, scarlet paint, and waiting lists measured in years.
makes.knownFor: V12 flagships, Formula 1, limited-run specials
makes.name: Ferrari
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: Ferruccio built tractors, got insulted by Enzo Ferrari, and answered with the Miura. Lamborghini has been the loud answer ever since, Countach posters defined a generation's bedroom walls.
makes.knownFor: Countach, V12 drama, wedge design
makes.name: Lamborghini
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: Gave the world the three-point seat belt and refused to patent it. Boxy wagons became a design language; the 240 simply refuses to die.
makes.knownFor: Safety, wagons, Scandinavian restraint
makes.name: Volvo
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Berthold Werner, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: The E-Type was called the most beautiful car ever made by Enzo Ferrari himself. Jaguar's history swings between genius and chaos, usually in the same decade.
makes.knownFor: E-Type, XK engines, Le Mans wins in the 1950s
makes.name: Jaguar
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Berthold Werner, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: The 1948 Series I was a stopgap built from war-surplus aluminium; it became the default vehicle of farms, armies, and expeditions on every continent.
makes.knownFor: Defender, Range Rover, expedition pedigree
makes.name: Land Rover
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Yu Chu Chin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: Toyota spent a billion dollars and five years building a Mercedes-beater in secret, then launched it in 1989 to a stunned industry. The luxury arm has been the quiet benchmark ever since, and built the LFA just to prove it could.
makes.knownFor: Quiet luxury, hybrid drivetrains, the LFA
makes.name: Lexus
makes.photoCredit: Photo: 先従隗始, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: Founded in Milan in 1910, Alfa won the first two Formula 1 world championships and employed a young Enzo Ferrari. The cars have always been emotional purchases, the Giulia Quadrifoglio is the current argument.
makes.knownFor: Racing pedigree, the Quadrifoglio, beautiful trouble
makes.name: Alfa Romeo
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Ermell, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: Lionel Martin raced specials at Aston Clinton hill climb; the company he founded in 1913 has gone bankrupt seven times and never stopped making the definitive British GT. Bond's DB5 made it immortal.
makes.knownFor: Grand tourers, the DB line, James Bond
makes.name: Aston Martin
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: Henry Leland built Cadillac on interchangeable parts and precision machining in 1902. It defined American luxury for a century, tailfins, the Escalade, and a Blackwing line that out-handles the Germans.
makes.knownFor: Escalade, V-Series, tailfins
makes.name: Cadillac
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Oleg Yunakov, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: The Dodge brothers started as machinists supplying Ford before building their own car in 1914. The modern brand distilled itself to one idea, horsepower, cheap, and the Hellcat era was its glorious peak.
makes.knownFor: Charger, Challenger, Hellcat horsepower
makes.name: Dodge
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Ermell, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: GM's truck-only division since 1911. GMC sells the same bones as Chevrolet trucks with a premium brief, Denali became a luxury brand inside the brand, and the Hummer EV gave it an electric halo.
makes.knownFor: Sierra, Yukon, the Denali trim
makes.name: GMC
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Alexander Migl, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: Korea's oldest carmaker spent decades as the budget option, then hired Peter Schreyer from Audi in 2006 and redesigned everything. The Stinger, Telluride, and EV6 are what the turnaround produced.
makes.knownFor: Telluride, EV6, design-led turnaround
makes.name: Kia
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Alexander Migl, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: Colin Chapman's doctrine, simplify, then add lightness, won seven Formula 1 constructors' titles and defined the British sports car. Now Geely-owned and electric-bound, with the Emira as the last petrol farewell.
makes.knownFor: Lightness, handling, Formula 1 heritage
makes.name: Lotus
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Thierry & Didier Descouens, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: Six brothers from Bologna, a trident borrowed from a Neptune statue, and a century of racing and grand touring. Maserati has lived under Citroën, De Tomaso, Ferrari, and now Stellantis, the cars kept their opera regardless.
makes.knownFor: The Trident, Quattroporte, Italian grand tourers
makes.name: Maserati
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: Bruce McLaren founded his race team in 1963; the road-car arm's first effort, the 1992 F1, is still the fastest naturally aspirated production car ever made. Everything since chases that standard in carbon fibre.
makes.knownFor: Formula 1, carbon tubs, the F1 road car
makes.name: McLaren
makes.photoCaption: F1 GTR Longtail (race car), rear view
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Ank Kumar, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: John Z. DeLorean left GM to build the car of the future: unpainted stainless panels, gullwing doors, and a factory in Dunmurry, Northern Ireland. One model, three model years, receivership in 1982, and, thanks to a time machine in a 1985 film, immortality.
makes.knownFor: The DMC-12, gullwing doors, stainless steel
makes.name: DeLorean
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Berthold Werner, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: Fred and August Duesenberg built racing engines good enough to win Indianapolis and Le Mans outright; under E.L. Cord from 1926 they built the Model J, the grandest American car of its age, sold as a bare chassis to coachbuilders. The marque died with the Cord empire in 1937. The cars never did.
makes.knownFor: Model J, coachbuilt luxury, straight-eight engines
makes.name: Duesenberg
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Michael Barera, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: 'Ask the man who owns one.' Founded in Warren, Ohio and Detroit-based from 1903, Packard was American luxury's default answer for half a century, Twin Sixes, straight-eights and Twelves built to the standard Rolls-Royce was measured against. A merger with Studebaker and a changing market ended it in 1958; the best Packards remain blue-chip classics.
makes.knownFor: The Twelve, the Caribbean, 'Ask the man who owns one'
makes.name: Packard
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Oleg Yunakov, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: An aircraft company that built cars like aircraft: teardrop bodies, two-stroke engines, front-wheel drive proven in Swedish snow, and turbocharging for everyone years before it was fashion. GM ownership ended in the 2011 bankruptcy; the faithful, and the cars, never really left.
makes.knownFor: Turbocharging, the 900, aircraft thinking
makes.name: Saab
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: Wagon-maker in 1852 and carmaker from 1902, Studebaker was America's great independent for six decades. Raymond Loewy's studio gave it the landmark 1953 coupes and the Avanti; the Lark nearly saved it. South Bend closed in 1963 and the last cars came from Canada in 1966, the designs aged better than the balance sheet.
makes.knownFor: Loewy coupes, the Avanti, the Lark
makes.name: Studebaker
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Michael Barera, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: Preston Tucker promised the car of tomorrow, today: rear-engined, a centre 'Cyclops Eye' headlight that steered with the wheels, and safety engineered in from the first sketch. Fifty-one cars were built before the company collapsed amid an SEC trial that ended in acquittal. The 48 is America's most famous almost.
makes.knownFor: The Tucker 48, Preston Tucker's rear-engined sedan
makes.name: Tucker
makes.photoCaption: Tucker 48 sedan 1948, front 3/4, Gilmore Car Museum
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Greg Gjerdingen, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: Born of the Nash–Hudson merger in 1954, American Motors survived by being cleverer than the giants: compacts when compacts weren't cool, the Javelin and AMX for the muscle years, and the Eagle, all-wheel drive for ordinary families, a generation before the crossover era. Chrysler absorbed AMC in 1987, mostly for Jeep.
makes.knownFor: Javelin, AMX, Gremlin, the Eagle
makes.name: AMC
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Michael Barera, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: GM's excitement division, by its own slogan and by the evidence: launched in 1926 as a companion to Oakland, it soon outsold its parent. The GTO started the muscle-car era in 1964, the Trans Am owned the late seventies, and the Solstice was a last flash of the old fire before GM closed the marque in 2010.
makes.knownFor: The GTO, the Trans Am, 'We Build Excitement'
makes.name: Pontiac
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Greg Gjerdingen, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: Ransom E. Olds founded the marque in 1897 and the Curved Dash made it America's first high-volume carmaker. The Rocket 88 put a modern overhead-valve V8 in a light body in 1949, the Toronado pioneered modern front-wheel drive, and the 4-4-2 carried the muscle years. GM phased Oldsmobile out in 2004, 107 years young.
makes.knownFor: The Curved Dash, Rocket 88, Toronado, 4-4-2
makes.name: Oldsmobile
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Michael Barera, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: Chrysler's value brand, launched in 1928, with a performance streak a mile wide: the Barracuda beat the Mustang to market by two weeks in 1964, the Road Runner made speed cheap, and the Hemi 'Cuda became the muscle market's ceiling. The Voyager helped invent the minivan in 1984. Chrysler retired the marque in 2001.
makes.knownFor: Road Runner, Barracuda, the Hemi 'Cuda, Voyager
makes.name: Plymouth
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Mustang Joe, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: E.L. Cord's own nameplate, built by Auburn: America's first front-wheel-drive production cars, and in the 810 a design so advanced the Museum of Modern Art put it on a pedestal. The empire fell in 1937. The cars never fell at all.
makes.knownFor: Front-wheel drive, the 810/812, E.L. Cord's empire
makes.name: Cord
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Wikimedia Commons contributor, CC BY-SA 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: Detroit's cleverest independent: the step-down body of 1948 put passengers inside the frame rails and made Hudsons handle like nothing else in America, and the Hornet's big six beat the V8s at their own game on the NASCAR circuit. Merged into AMC in 1954; the name ended in 1957.
makes.knownFor: The step-down design, the Hornet, Twin H-Power
makes.name: Hudson
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Тимба, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: Charles Nash built the industry's quiet innovator: overhead-valve engines, unit bodies, reclining seats, and in the 1950 Rambler, America's first successful compact. Nash merged with Hudson to form AMC in 1954, and its Rambler idea became the new company's whole future.
makes.knownFor: Overhead-valve engines, the Rambler, unit construction
makes.name: Nash
makes.photoCredit: Photo: CZmarlin, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: Shipbuilder Henry J. Kaiser took on Detroit from the world's largest factory building, with partner Joseph Frazer: for one year, 1947, Kaiser-Frazer outsold every other independent. The cars were handsome, the six was honest, and the Big Three's scale won in the end. US car production ended in 1955.
makes.knownFor: Post-war challenger, the Henry J, the Darrin sports car
makes.name: Kaiser
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Stephen Foskett, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: Harry Stutz debuted at Indianapolis in 1911 and finished eleventh with no mechanical trouble, 'the car that made good in a day.' The Bearcat made the marque; the Vertical Eight and the twin-cam DV-32 kept it at the luxury summit until 1937.
makes.knownFor: The Bearcat, the DV-32, 'the car that made good in a day'
makes.name: Stutz
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Katherine Tompkins, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: A bicycle company that became Britain's sports-car export champion: the TR line sold the open two-seater to America for three decades, the Stag aimed at Mercedes, and the Dolomite Sprint quietly invented the mass-produced sixteen-valve engine. Car production ended in 1984; the name survives with BMW.
makes.knownFor: The TR sports cars, the Stag, the Dolomite Sprint
makes.name: Triumph
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Daniel Milner, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: Born in a single evening at the 1952 Earls Court show: Donald Healey's sports car, Austin's engines and factories. The Big Healeys ruled early-sixties rallying, the Frogeye Sprite put a smile on the cheapest sports car in Britain, and the badge partnership ended in 1971.
makes.knownFor: The Big Healeys, the Frogeye Sprite, rally wins
makes.name: Austin-Healey
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Peter & Laila, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: The Jensen brothers' West Bromwich works built bodies for half the industry, then their own cars: fibreglass GTs first, then the Interceptor, Italian styling, American V8, and in the FF the world's first four-wheel-drive, anti-lock-braked production car. Production ended in 1976.
makes.knownFor: The Interceptor, the FF, Chrysler V8 grand tourers
makes.name: Jensen
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: Trevor Wilkinson started TVR in a Blackpool wheelwright's shop; under Peter Wheeler it became British sports-car making at its most gloriously uncompromising, glassfibre bodies, backbone chassis, enormous power-to-weight and a standing refusal of driver aids. The factory closed in 2006.
makes.knownFor: Glassfibre sports cars, the Griffith, no driver aids
makes.name: TVR
makes.photoCaption: 1961 TVR Grantura Mark IIA, front left (Hershey 2019)
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Mr.choppers, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: Herbert Austin built the Seven that motorised Britain, then the Longbridge works carried the Mini, the 1100 and the Metro, the cars ordinary Britain actually drove. The marque faded through the BMC and British Leyland years and was retired in the late 1980s.
makes.knownFor: The Seven, the Mini, Britain's everyday cars
makes.name: Austin
makes.photoCredit: Photo: DeFacto, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: Carl F. W. Borgward built Germany's most inventive post-war car group, the first new German design of 1949, the Isabella, air suspension on the P100, then lost it all in the sudden, still-argued collapse of 1961.
makes.knownFor: The Isabella, post-war German innovation, the 1961 collapse
makes.name: Borgward
makes.photoCredit: Photo: User Spurzem on de.wikipedia, CC BY-SA 2.0 de, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: Alejandro de Tomaso, an Argentine racer settled in Modena, built the formula that defined the marque for thirty years: Italian design, a mid-mounted Ford V8, and American dealer reach. The Pantera sold from 1971 to 1992.
makes.knownFor: The Pantera, Ford V8s in Italian chassis
makes.name: De Tomaso
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Andrew Bone from Weymouth, England, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: Jean Daninos turned a pressings company into France's last luxury marque: Chrysler V8s, hand-finished cabins, and a client list of kings and film stars. The Facellia's fragile engine sank the firm; production ended in October 1964.
makes.knownFor: Chrysler-powered French luxury GTs, the HK500 and Facel II
makes.name: Facel Vega
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: Renzo Rivolta's company licensed the Isetta to BMW, then aimed the other way entirely: Bertone-bodied grand tourers with Chevrolet and Ford V8s. The Grifo is the peak, Bizzarrini engineering under one of the great GT shapes.
makes.knownFor: The Grifo, Corvette-engined GTs, the Isetta's creator
makes.name: Iso
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Charles from Port Chester, New York, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: A knitting-machine and motorcycle giant that bet the company on Felix Wankel's rotary engine: first in the little Spider, then in the Ro80, 1968's European Car of the Year. Engine warranties consumed NSU; Volkswagen absorbed it into Audi in 1969.
makes.knownFor: The Wankel rotary, Spider and Ro80, and the Prinz
makes.name: NSU
makes.photoCredit: Photo: MrWalkr, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: Panhard & Levassor set the automobile's layout in 1891, engine front, drive rear, then reinvented itself after the war around tiny air-cooled flat-twins, front-wheel drive and radical economy. Citroën absorbed the marque and ended its cars in 1967.
makes.knownFor: The Système Panhard, flat-twin economy cars, Monte Carlo 1961
makes.name: Panhard
makes.photoCaption: 1952 Panhard Dyna X 120 Canadienne in Bremen, front left
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Andrew Bone from Weymouth, England, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: Founded to build Fiats in France, Simca became the country's second carmaker on the Aronde, bought Ford's French V8 works, pioneered the hatchback with the 1100, and faded through Chrysler and Peugeot ownership by 1970.
makes.knownFor: The Aronde, the 1000 Rallye, the hatchback 1100
makes.name: Simca
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Philmarin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: Anthony Lago took over Talbot's French works and built the summit of the French classics: Figoni-teardrop coupés before the war, a Le Mans winner after it. The America of 1955 was the last car; Simca absorbed the firm in 1959.
makes.knownFor: The teardrop T150C-SS, the Le Mans-winning T26 Grand Sport
makes.name: Talbot-Lago
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Joe Ross from Lansing, Michigan, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

makes.blurb: Willys-Overland built the wartime Jeep and spent the peace turning it civilian: the CJ, the all-steel station wagon that prefigured the SUV, and the Aero saloon. Kaiser bought the company in 1953; the Willys name left its grilles in the 1960s.
makes.knownFor: The Jeep, MB, CJ, and the first all-steel wagon
makes.name: Willys
makes.photoCredit: Photo: Greg Gjerdingen from Willmar, USA, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

note: Marque registry. Model counts are derived at build time into search-index.json; see COVERAGE.md for what is seeded and what is planned.
